title: Choosing a stylist, braider or loctician
question_forms: How do I find a stylist, braider or loctician who knows my hair?
What should I ask a stylist or loctician before booking?
tradition_says: Find someone who specialises in natural hair, ideally recommended by people whose hair you admire; a stylist who knows textured hair will look after your scalp and hair better.

layer1.plain_answer: No study shows that a stylist's training or specialism gives better hair or scalp outcomes. In one small US survey, most Black cosmetologists had never heard of two scarring hair-loss conditions. Book a consultation or a simple wash first, watch how they handle your hair, and tell them when a style hurts.

do.text: Book a consultation or a simple wash and condition first, to see how they handle your hair before a long service.

source.name: Going Natural, "How to select a natural hairstylist" (a natural-hair blog)

do.text: Ask about their experience with your hair type, the products they use and the price before you book.

source.name: Going Natural, "How to select a natural hairstylist" (a natural-hair blog)

do.text: Have braids put in by a trained, qualified professional, and relaxers by a trained, experienced one.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

do.text: Say so if it hurts: scalp pain after installation means braids are probably too tight.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

do.text: For locs, ask a loctician how often to retwist: one booking site says about every 4 weeks for starter locs and every 8 to 12 weeks or more for mature locs, and that retwisting too often can cause thinning and breakage.

source.name: StyleSeat (a booking platform), "How often should you retwist locs" (loctician tips credited to Tara Cline; no qualifications listed)

avoid.text: Expecting your stylist to spot scalp disease: in one survey most cosmetologists had not heard of lichen planopilaris or CCCA.

see_someone_when: Hair loss, bald patches, or a scalp that is sore, itchy or scaly: a doctor, for a dermatology referral, not a stylist.
A stylist or braider tells you to see a doctor about your scalp (doctor or dermatologist).
A hairline that keeps moving back (doctor or dermatologist).

tested.finding: 78.9% had never heard of lichen planopilaris and 57.9% had never heard of CCCA. All reported avoiding or limiting tight braids or locs and tight ponytails or buns; 89.5% avoided tight weaves. 94.7% (18 of 19) had referred a client to a dermatologist in the past year. The authors say there are gaps in knowledge of hair loss risk factors.
tested.note: Tiny self-selected survey; says nothing about outcomes of using a trained stylist.

tested.population: Stylist or loctician training and client outcomes
tested.design: PubMed search run 12 Nov 2026, exact string: (hairdresser OR stylist OR cosmetologist OR loctician) AND ("natural hair" OR afro-textured OR "African American") AND (training OR knowledge OR referral) (result count 25).
tested.finding: My search found nothing on outcomes: of 25 results I read the first 8 titles; one is the cosmetologist survey above (PMID 40654542), one a knowledge-gaps paper (Douglas 2024, PMID 38197981, title read, abstract empty in PubMed), the rest salon-based health-promotion or unrelated. None compares hair or scalp outcomes by stylist training. Control: PubMed search "Khumalo NP AND hair" returned 71 results on the same day.

tier_driver: That a stylist, braider or loctician who specialises in afro hair gives better hair and scalp results: no study of outcomes by stylist found.
tier_note: D because the claim has no outcome study; the cosmetologist survey is a B line about knowledge, not results. A trial or cohort comparing outcomes by stylist training would move it.
harm_note: No harm signal found. Hidden risk: tight installation by any stylist is a traction risk (BAD, other entries).
evidence_summary: The guidance is general. The BAD leaflet asks for trained, qualified or experienced professionals for braids and relaxers but gives no criteria for choosing one. A natural-hair blog suggests asking for recommendations, booking a consultation or a wash first, checking how the stylist handles your hair, and asking about experience with your hair type, products and cost. The only study found is a 19-person survey of Black cosmetologists: they avoided tight styles, nearly all had referred a client to a dermatologist, but most did not know two scarring conditions.
gaps: Untested: outcomes by stylist training; a reliable directory; how to judge a loctician or braider for scalp safety. I opened one loctician-specific page (StyleSeat, a booking platform, with no author credentials and a single quoted loctician; it is added as common advice) but no clinical, training-body or outcome source; earlier I did not open a loctician-specific source (a YouTube search found loctician advice videos but the caption download was rate-limited, so none was read). Reddit not read (snippets only). Closes the 12 Nov partial as "common advice from one blog; no outcome study".
